_note: Quiz and true-or-false items written but not yet blind-checked; apply_check.py moves checked items onto the site.

item.statement: Most people who try cocaine become dependent on it.
item.why: In a big US survey, about 21 in 100 people who had tried cocaine were expected to become dependent at some point. The figures rest on people's own memories.

item.statement: Most Vietnam veterans who got over heroin addiction did it through treatment.
item.why: Fewer than 2 in 100 men who'd used narcotics in Vietnam entered drug treatment back home, and those who did relapsed as often as civilian patients.

item.statement: Most people who were ever dependent on cocaine were still dependent decades later.
item.why: In a US survey, half had recovered within about 4 years, though some stayed dependent for decades. Recovery here means not counting as dependent for a year, not quitting.

item.statement: Of people who try them, a bigger share become dependent on tobacco than on cocaine.
item.why: In one US survey, about 68 in 100 people who'd smoked a full cigarette were expected to become dependent, against 21 in 100 for cocaine. These are projections from people's memories.

item.statement: Most US soldiers addicted to heroin in Vietnam stayed addicted after coming home.
item.why: Of the men addicted in Vietnam, 5 in 100 were addicted again in their first year home and 12 in 100 within 3 years. Vietnam's conditions were unusual.

item.statement: People got over cocaine and cannabis dependence faster than alcohol or cigarette dependence.
item.why: In a US survey, half had recovered within about 4 years for cocaine and 6 for cannabis, against 16 for alcohol and 30 for cigarettes. Recovery here means not counting as dependent for a year, not quitting.

item.statement: Scientists have measured how MDMA affects peeing.
item.why: No study has. They measured a water-holding hormone and blood salt instead, and the one team that collected urine never reported what it found.

item.statement: All the studies found that MDMA raises the hormone that holds in water.
item.why: Not all: it rose in one small study of 8 men, but three studies with a dummy pill found no rise in it or its marker. None of them reported anything about pee.

item.statement: In the rat study, heroin was deadlier in a room the rats had never seen.
item.why: Every rat knew both rooms. Heroin killed about 64 in 100 rats in the room linked with dummy injections, against 32 in 100 in the room linked with heroin. Rats aren't people.

item.statement: It's been shown in people that a new place makes overdose more likely.
item.why: In people there's only one study: 10 overdose survivors' memories, with nobody to compare them with. And in the rat study, both rooms were familiar to the rats.

item.statement: An online pill report with a photo is more likely to be right.
item.why: In a Dutch check against lab tests, a photo helped match a report to the right pill. But reports with photos were not less often dangerously wrong: far too little MDMA, or a drug left out.

item.statement: Online pill reports more often claim too much MDMA than too little.
item.why: Checked against Dutch lab tests in 2014–15, about 40 in 100 reports said over 10 mg too much and 18 in 100 over 10 mg too little. That's two websites in one country.

item.statement: Blotters taken as LSD always hold LSD.
item.why: In some reported cases, blotters taken as 'acid' held an NBOMe instead. Nobody has counted how often this happens.

item.statement: Published NBOMe cases had far more seizures than poison centre cases.
item.why: About 38 in 100 published cases had seizures, against 4 in 100 of 25 cases at Texas poison centres. Published cases are often the worst ones.

item.statement: Most deaths linked to designer benzos involved no other drug.
item.why: In a review of published cases, 115 of 141 death entries also listed an opioid, and only 3 listed no other drug.

item.statement: Designer benzos have been shown to be riskier than prescribed benzos.
item.why: Nobody has compared them. The reports only count people who got into trouble, so they can't say how risky one use is.

item.statement: Studies show a hole in the nose from snorting closes up once you stop.
item.why: None of these studies followed people after they stopped. Experts think stopping is the only known way to halt the damage, but that's opinion.

item.statement: Snorting cocaine can damage the roof of your mouth, not just your nose.
item.why: In 17 published case series, about 30 in 100 people with this damage had it in the roof of the mouth. Nobody knows how many people who snort get it.

item.statement: Most people would pick Valium over a dummy pill.
item.why: In a lab study, most young volunteers without drug problems chose the dummy pill. It was one small study, and people with a history of drug problems did choose benzos in other studies.

item.statement: People with anxiety liked Valium more than others in a lab test.
item.why: In one small study, anxious volunteers neither chose nor liked it more, though it eased their anxiety. Studies that let anxious people take it as needed did find a preference.

item.statement: Most people who misuse benzos say they do it to get high.
item.why: In a big US survey, 12 in 100 named getting high as their main reason. Relaxing (47 in 100) and sleep (27) came first, by people's own account.

item.statement: Most people who misuse benzos are hooked on them.
item.why: In a big US survey, about 7 in 100 people who misused benzos met the criteria for dependence. 'Misuse' there includes taking your own pills more often than prescribed.

item.statement: In death records, people who had temazepam too died with less alcohol in their blood.
item.why: In Finland: 2.5 parts per thousand in the middle, against 3.3 in deaths from alcohol alone. But only deaths were counted, and the groups were different people, so it can't show the risk.

item.statement: In death records, people with more temazepam had died with less alcohol in their blood.
item.why: Among 57 Finnish deaths with both, those with more temazepam had died at lower alcohol levels still. Only deaths were counted, so this can't show how risky mixing is.

item.statement: Scientists know just how much Suboxone it takes to block other opioids.
item.why: The researchers behind the brain scans say nobody knows. The levels in their summary came from early modelling of a few volunteers.

item.statement: In one US study, about 5 in 100 had a doctor treat an overdose within 6 months of stopping Suboxone.
item.why: 464 of 8,996 people on Medicaid who stopped after 6 to 18 months did. People who died were left out, so fatal overdoses aren't counted.

item.statement: People who stayed on Suboxone longer had fewer overdoses after they stopped.
item.why: In one large US study, about 5 in 100 had an overdose treated by a doctor, whether they'd been on it 6 or 18 months. A small difference could have been missed.

item.statement: In a US survey, over 1 in 3 people who took buprenorphine (as in Suboxone) after fentanyl remembered severe withdrawal.
item.why: 250 of 685 did (37 in 100), against 15 in 100 after methadone. These were memories, and the survey couldn't tell withdrawal buprenorphine caused from withdrawal it didn't ease.

item.statement: With too much tramadol, seizures only happen if other drugs were taken too.
item.why: In one Australian study, 2 of 20 people who took only tramadol had seizures, against 6 of 51 who took other pills too. These were overdoses, not normal doses.

item.statement: Too much tramadol won't affect your breathing.
item.why: In one Australian study of 71 overdoses, 18 in 100 people had breathing trouble with low oxygen. Many had taken other pills too.

item.statement: When people stop tramadol, it always feels like the usual opioid withdrawal.
item.why: In US reports from 1995 to 2000, about 1 in 8 cases also had panic, confusion, numbness or hallucinations. These were reported cases only, so how often it happens is unknown.

item.statement: Studies show people quit Adderall over side effects far more often than Ritalin.
item.why: Across short trials, quitting over side effects wasn't clearly different between amphetamine and methylphenidate, though a gap wasn't ruled out.

item.statement: Starting Adderall instead of Ritalin doubles the risk of psychosis.
item.why: In one big records study it was about 1.65 times the rate, about 1 extra case per 1,000 people a year. 'Twice' came from leaving out that amphetamine starters were followed longer.

item.statement: In a trial, many 'side effects' blamed on ADHD pills were there before the kids took any.
item.why: In one blinded trial, parents called 82 in 100 children irritable before any medicine was given.

item.statement: Psychosis is rare in people who start prescribed ADHD pills.
item.why: In a big records study of young people with ADHD, about 2 to 3 in 1,000 a year had a new psychotic episode treated with medicine. That's one study.

item.statement: The detection times on drug-test charts come from big studies.
item.why: Each figure in one review came from one small study, some of just one or two people given one dose. Another chart came from textbooks, older reviews and lab websites.

item.statement: A positive drug screen always means the person took that drug.
item.why: Screens use antibodies that can react to some medicines, like efavirenz on one benzo test. Most reports are single cases. Both reviews say a different lab method should check a screen.

item.statement: Amoxicillin can make a cocaine test positive.
item.why: A clinical review found no evidence behind this popular claim. It says numbing drugs like lidocaine don't trip cocaine tests either.

item.statement: If weed shows up again after a negative test, the person smoked again.
item.why: On a locked ward where nobody could smoke, positives often came back after a negative. That's one study of 60 regular smokers.

item.statement: Taking MDMA with LSD pushes heart rate and blood pressure higher than LSD alone.
item.why: In a lab study of 24 people, they rose about as high as on MDMA alone. Body temperature wasn't clearly higher.

item.statement: Death rates were about the same in and out of methadone treatment.
item.why: In 16 groups of people on methadone, about 11 in 1,000 died each year in treatment, against about 36 out of it. People who leave differ in other ways, so this can't show cause.

item.statement: You can't die from opioid withdrawal.
item.why: Deaths have been reported, all in jail; one editorial suggests untreated vomiting and diarrhoea can dry the body out. How often it happens is unknown.

item.statement: Given LSD or the drug in magic mushrooms without being told which, most people can't tell which one it was.
item.why: In a 28-person lab study, people named the right drug after 71 to 86 in 100 sessions, though they rated the trips alike on most measures.

item.statement: Adding MDMA to LSD has been shown to make a bad trip less likely.
item.why: In a lab study of 24 people in a calm hospital room, bad-feeling and fear scores weren't clearly lower than on LSD alone.

item.statement: In a lab test, people rated trips on LSD and on psilocybin, the drug in magic mushrooms, as much alike.
item.why: In 28 people, the ratings barely differed. But that's no proof they're the same, and most could tell which drug they'd had.

item.statement: Indica and sativa labels tell you which smell compounds your weed has.
item.why: In 41,201 US lab-tested samples, the labels barely matched the mix of smell compounds (terpenes). The labels came from a strain website, not the bags, and effects weren't measured.

item.statement: Almost all weed tested from licensed growers in six US states was THC-rich, not CBD-rich.
item.why: In six US states, 94 to 97 in 100 lab-tested flower samples from licensed growers had at least five times as much THC as CBD.

item.statement: In studies, death rates were highest in the first weeks after leaving methadone.
item.why: In 5 studies, deaths in the first 4 weeks off methadone ran at about 32 a year per 1,000 people, against about 14 later on. People who leave may differ in other ways.
